highlights.content: Indian AI startup SquadStack.ai has launched Maya, which it describes as the world's first Sales Large Language Model (LLM), claiming it outperformed models from OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Alibaba and NVIDIA in a benchmark designed to evaluate AI performance in sales conversations. Maya scored 96.7% on the company’s in-house SquadStack Telesales LLM Benchmark, ahead of Google's Gemma 4 31B (92.5%), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (92.2%) and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna (89%), the company said. “SquadStack.ai post-trained it from an open-weight foundation model on more than 40 crore real sales interactions from six years of running sales calls, each tagged with how the call ended: a sale, a callback or a drop-off,” SquadStack.ai said in a release. The company added that Maya is designed to understand the nuances of Indian sales conversations, including informal responses, hesitation and interruptions. It currently handles more than 50 lakh conversations daily across Hinglish and Indian languages. To evaluate the models, SquadStack.ai created a benchmark using 9,962 conversational moments from 471 real sales calls. Eleven models were assessed on their ability to generate the next response in a conversation. Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 was used as a neutral judge to evaluate responses against seven parameters, including maintaining the conversation's objective and using tools correctly. According to the company, Maya maintained conversational context on 96% of turns, compared with 90% for the next-best model, and selected the appropriate response 95% of the time against 87% for its closest rival. "A live sales call is the hardest place to run an LLM. Thousands of calls can start in the same second, and the customer hears every slow turn. So we built Maya for this one job, with the sales behaviour in its weights rather than in a long prompt," said Vikas Gulati, co-founder and CTO of SquadStack.ai. Maya is the second model developed by the company's in-house model factory, following its speech recognition model, Arth V2. SquadStack.ai said Maya is built and hosted in India, ensuring that customer conversations remain within the country. Accelerator specifications describe the potential performance of individual components. Time to target quality shows how the complete system performs on an actual training workload. For customers, faster time to target quality translates to higher performance, more experiments within the same development window, better use of costly GPU capacity, and greater confidence that large training jobs will finish on schedule. At production scale, improvements in training efficiency can remove days from a run and materially reduce infrastructure costs. We submitted [NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72](https://www.coreweave.com/products/nvidia-vera-rubin) and [NVIDIA GB200 NVL72](https://www.coreweave.com/products/nvidia-blackwell) results in the Closed division’s Available category. At the same GPU count, our NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 submission took 48.40 minutes, a 2.7x improvement in time to train.¹ We were the only cloud provider to submit multi-rack Vera Rubin results in this round.² ![Bar chart comparing DeepSeek-V3 time to target quality, showing NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 reaching the target in approximately 18 minutes versus 48 minutes for NVIDIA GB200 NVL72.](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/62bc66d283fd9c34ffec780a/6afa2ac7aebdfc07f5d5e9e8_figure1_deepseek_v3_time_to_target_quality.png) DeepSeek-V3 time to target quality on Vera Rubin NVL72 vs GB200 NVL72 This benchmark is especially relevant for teams training large MoE models. CAMPBELL, CA, UNITED STATES, November 15, 2026 /[EINPresswire.com](https://www.einpresswire.com/)/ — [StudioX AI](https://studiox-ai.com) today announced the availability of Agent2Agent ([A2A](https://a2a-protocol.org/)) interoperability for air-gapped enterprise deployments. The new capability lets compatible AI agents hand off work and return results within an organization’s isolated network. Enterprises can use it to build agentic AI applications that coordinate work across internal systems and teams. Enterprise workflows can span systems that different departments manage. In a manufacturing plant, for example, a maintenance app could receive an equipment alert and ask a parts inventory agent to check whether a replacement is in stock. The inventory agent would return its findings, and the maintenance app could combine them with service history to prepare a work order for a supervisor’s approval. Each team can keep using the systems it manages while its agent contributes to the same workflow. “An enterprise may already have agents built by different teams for different jobs. A StudioX assistant or multi-agent workflow, called a Mission, can be published as an A2A agent with an Agent Card that describes the tasks it can handle. A compatible agent built on another platform can use that information to send work to StudioX and receive the result. In an air-gapped deployment, participating agents and the services they rely on, including models, identity services, and data sources, need to be reachable within the isolated environment. StudioX AI lets teams build a full-stack application around those handoffs, with an interface for reviewing results, a record of the steps the agent took, and approval points for decisions that require human sign-off. We present empirical evidence from state-of-the-art models exhibiting behaviors consistent with in-context search, and explore methods for producing Meta-CoT via process supervision, synthetic data generation, and search algorithms. Finally, we outline a concrete pipeline for training a model to produce Meta-CoTs, incorporating instruction tuning with linearized search traces and reinforcement learning post-training. Finally, we discuss open research questions, including scaling laws, verifier roles, and the potential for discovering novel reasoning algorithms. In this paper, we focus on the related problem of recovering IRT-based difficulty when the data originally reported item p-value (percent correct responses). We model this item difficulty using a repository of reading passages and student data from US standardized tests from New York and Texas for grades 3-8 spanning the years 2017-23. AI Agents.content: - Artificial Intelligence - 4 min read # Why enterprise AI success takes more than deploying a few AI agents Organizations are increasingly adopting multi-agent AI systems, which can improve business outcomes but may weaken ethical standards. Leaders must establish governed AI operating models to address these challenges effectively. It is essential for enterprises to ensure their AI agents make trustworthy decisions aligned with organizational objectives. Upcoming enterprises will need to emphasize accountability and governance as AI becomes more autonomous. When companies think about AI risk today, most of the focus remains at the model level: Can the LLM hallucinate? Will it follow policies? Does our information remain confidential? These are all important questions that we need to ask. As AI becomes more prevalent in our lives, leaders need to expand their view of risks. As organisations move from singular AI agents to multiple copilots’ networks of specialized AI agents, the challenge is no longer understanding singular agents but how groups of AI agents behave when they work together. This bifurcation can become wider with AI agents. In a supply chain scenario, one agent might overlook demand, another optimize pricing, another identify cost savings and another create an execution plan. While these specializations can make work faster, it doesn’t automatically mean alignment. An agent improving margins might overlook customer trust, while one reducing costs may miss service impacts. An agent reviewing the final output may check whether the task was completed without considering if the recommendation aligns with the organisation's objectives. **The next management challenge of enterprise AI** Smart agents alone will not be enough to manage these risks. Enterprises will need a governed AI operating model. This is where a governed AI operating model becomes important, one designed to make enterprise planning and execution more agile, adaptive and autonomous without losing sight of accountability. But autonomy without governance does not amount to transformation. It can simply mean that risk scales alongside automation. If AI agents were to optimize individual tasks without context of the enterprise data, they would produce much faster and more sophisticated recommendations that should not be trusted without verification. Leadership therefore needs to move beyond asking, "How many AI agents do we have?" and start asking, "Can we trust the decisions our AI organisation is making?" **The path forward requires a different architecture** Prompts by themselves are not enough to give AI agents the guidance they require. Business standards, operating regulations, financial considerations, legal needs, customer promises, and escalation levels are all parts of a shared system that organisations require to function. This enables AI agents to operate as an interconnected, cohesive decision-making system. Clear decision-making rights are also needed for these enterprises. Leaders need to specify which decisions should be automated, which require human interaction and which will not need AI automation. Additionally, the workflow itself also requires governance. Controls must function at the same pace as decision-making becomes increasingly independent. Leaders should be able to track the information being used, the assumptions they make, the risks they identify and the logic behind their decisions. This helps companies move from unregulated adoption to well-established and disciplined AI management by establishing a continuous learning loop. AI Agents.titleZh: Agentic AI: New Frontiers in Computing, Mathematical Reasoning, and Scientific Discovery | UMD Department of Computer Science
AI Agents.content: # Agentic AI: New Frontiers in Computing, Mathematical Reasoning, and Scientific Discovery Recent advances in artificial intelligence are transforming not only how we solve computational problems, but also how we formulate research questions, develop algorithms, and discover new knowledge. As AI evolves from a tool for individual tasks into autonomous agents capable of reasoning, coding, experimentation, and verification, we are approaching a fundamental shift in the practice of computational and scientific research. In this talk, I will discuss emerging opportunities and challenges at the intersection of agentic AI, computer science, and applied mathematics. A central theme is the evolving relationship between human and artificial intelligence: while AI can increasingly scale the generation of ideas, algorithms, experiments, and mathematical arguments, scientific judgment, rigorous verification, and trustworthy reasoning remain critical bottlenecks. I will highlight three emerging paradigms—agentic computing, autonomous scientific discovery, and agentic theorem proving—and discuss the new algorithmic and mathematical foundations they demand. I will conclude with a research outlook on trustworthy autonomous agents, efficient AI-driven computation, multi-agent collaboration, and AI-enabled scientific discovery. These directions point toward a future in which AI does more than accelerate existing research workflows: it fundamentally expands what we can compute, reason about, and discover.

AI Agents.content: ## Artificial Intelligence # Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts. The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production. Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk. In this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture. ## Multi-agent coordination patterns Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path. In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work. ### Tier 1: Patterns (deterministic control flow) **1.1 Sequential Pipeline:** Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage. **1.2 Conditional Workflow:** Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path. In the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post. **1.3 Conditional Router**: A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage. The following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point. **1.4 Parallel Workflow:** A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces. LLMs.titleZh: SquadStack.ai launches Maya, claims its Sales LLM outperforms models from OpenAI, Google - The Economic Times
LLMs.content: Indian AI startup SquadStack.ai has launched Maya, which it describes as the world's first Sales Large Language Model (LLM), claiming it outperformed models from OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Alibaba and NVIDIA in a benchmark designed to evaluate AI performance in sales conversations. Maya scored 96.7% on the company’s in-house SquadStack Telesales LLM Benchmark, ahead of Google's Gemma 4 31B (92.5%), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (92.2%) and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna (89%), the company said. “SquadStack.ai post-trained it from an open-weight foundation model on more than 40 crore real sales interactions from six years of running sales calls, each tagged with how the call ended: a sale, a callback or a drop-off,” SquadStack.ai said in a release. The company added that Maya is designed to understand the nuances of Indian sales conversations, including informal responses, hesitation and interruptions. It currently handles more than 50 lakh conversations daily across Hinglish and Indian languages. To evaluate the models, SquadStack.ai created a benchmark using 9,962 conversational moments from 471 real sales calls. Eleven models were assessed on their ability to generate the next response in a conversation. Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 was used as a neutral judge to evaluate responses against seven parameters, including maintaining the conversation's objective and using tools correctly. According to the company, Maya maintained conversational context on 96% of turns, compared with 90% for the next-best model, and selected the appropriate response 95% of the time against 87% for its closest rival. "A live sales call is the hardest place to run an LLM. Thousands of calls can start in the same second, and the customer hears every slow turn. So we built Maya for this one job, with the sales behaviour in its weights rather than in a long prompt," said Vikas Gulati, co-founder and CTO of SquadStack.ai. Maya is the second model developed by the company's in-house model factory, following its speech recognition model, Arth V2. SquadStack.ai said Maya is built and hosted in India, ensuring that customer conversations remain within the country. This, it said, could help banks, lenders and insurers address data protection requirements under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act. The company is also developing systems to improve the model through insights from live calls, with plans to incorporate cues such as pauses, changes in tone and a customer's previous interactions. LLMs.title: Pediatric Neurology Benchmark Finds Significant Performance Variation
LLMs.titleZh: Pediatric Neurology Benchmark Finds Significant Performance Variation
LLMs.content: In a prospective, blinded benchmarking study evaluating artificial intelligence for pediatric neurology patient education, linear mixed-effects models revealed significant performance variation across four large language models (F(3,27) = 8.76, p < 0.001). Effective patient education is critical in pediatric neurology care, yet healthcare teams frequently face substantial consultation time constraints alongside variable health literacy among families. While large language models present a scalable solution for drafting educational materials, their factual accuracy and safety profiles within this highly specialized clinical domain have remained incompletely evaluated. To rigorously assess model capabilities, investigators developed a prospective benchmarking protocol analyzing model responses to ten standardized pediatric neurology prompts across four platforms, generating 40 distinct scenario-model pairs. A blinded panel consisting of seven consultant pediatric neurology evaluators appraised the generated texts using an expert-developed rubric covering factual accuracy, safety, clinical appropriateness, and usability, relying on median scores across raters for all primary comparisons. DeepSeek attained the highest overall composite performance score at 4.01 ± 0.61 while triggering zero safety flags, and it also secured the highest System Usability Scale rating at 74.2 out of 100. ChatGPT recorded a moderate overall composite score of 3.72 ± 0.75, and statistical analysis showed that the composite score difference between DeepSeek and ChatGPT was not statistically significant (p = 0.087). Safety evaluations demonstrated notable hazards among the generated responses, with ChatGPT responsible for the majority of identified issues, accounting for five of the eight total safety flags recorded, which included a contraindicated medication recommendation. In comparison, Gemini and Perplexity achieved lower overall composite ratings, averaging 3.45 ± 0.77 and 3.38 ± 0.71, respectively. The benchmark further demonstrated that the presence of even a single consensus safety flag dramatically undermined specialist confidence in the content. Across the evaluation cohort, the occurrence of any consensus safety flag reduced the odds of expert approval for caregiver-facing deployment after clinical review by more than ninety percent (odds ratio: 0.08, p < 0.001). The authors stressed that the reported conclusions remain confined to the specific clinical prompts evaluated and do not establish generalized safety, clinical efficacy, real-world decision support, or direct caregiver comprehension, noting that no patient families or caregivers were directly examined. Consequently, the research team concluded that no current language model is equipped for autonomous healthcare communication, making mandatory clinician oversight an indispensable safeguard. Methodologically, the prospective investigation relied on a structured evaluation architecture designed to test model behavior under controlled, blinded conditions. Seven consultant pediatric neurology specialists evaluated the responses generated by the four artificial intelligence platforms across ten standardized clinical prompts, resulting in forty distinct scenario-model pairs. Rather than relying on unstandardized impressions, the blinded raters utilized an expert-developed rubric specifically structured to measure four core parameters: factual accuracy, clinical safety, appropriateness, and perceived usability. LLMs.content: UPDATED 18:48 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026 ### Corma raises $125M to train cybersecurity-optimized foundation models Corma.ai Ltd., a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for cybersecurity teams, has raised $125 million in funding. NEA led the Series A round. Corma stated today that returning backers Khosla Ventures, Coatue and Sequoia Capital chipped in as well. The company is now valued at $1 billion. Corma, which has offices in San Francisco and Tel Aviv, says that competing AI models are often better at launching cyberattacks than fixing them. The company recently conducted a test in which it asked several large language models to hack a simulated corporate network. They succeeded at installing a malicious file across 85% of the test runs. In contrast, the models found only 12% of the malicious files that they themselves installed. According to Corma, the gap between LLMs’ offensive and defensive capabilities can give hackers an edge over cybersecurity teams. That’s the issue the company is tackling with its cybersecurity-optimized AI models. Corma says that the algorithms can speed up some breach response workflows by a factor of 100 while reducing the associated costs. The company benchmarked one of its models against the competition using an evaluation called DefenseBench V5. The test measures two metrics: how reliably a model performs defensive cybersecurity tasks and how fast it completes them. Corma says that its model outperformed GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and several other cutting-edge LLMs. The company’s algorithms find breaches by analyzing data from other cybersecurity tools. Corma can ingest telemetry generated by firewalls, network monitoring software and a range of other applications. The company says that its models not only find threats but also generate remediation guidance for each one. Automating breach response tasks is difficult because it requires LLMs to filter numerous false positives and duplicate alerts. Moreover, models often have access to only partial information about breaches. Many companies discard cybersecurity logs after a relatively short amount of time to reduce data storage costs. Corma says that its algorithms can perform breach investigations on a fully autonomous basis. If human input is needed, they alert a relevant member of the cybersecurity team. It’s also possible to manually steer Corma’s models via a Slack chatbot. An administrator could, for example, ask Corma to double-check whether a recent effort to remove malware from a compromised server was successful. “Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand,” said Corma co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Alon Pluda. That shift is changing which companies matter. Author: Tencent Tech, Xiao Jing On November 15, Deedy Das (@deedydas), a partner at veteran Silicon Valley venture capital firm Menlo Ventures, shared a global ranking of AI company valuations and revenues on social media. Founded in 1976, Menlo Ventures is one of the oldest venture capital firms in Silicon Valley, having invested in well-known tech companies such as Uber and Chime. In recent years, the firm has focused on AI as a key investment area and released the widely circulated "State of Generative AI in the Enterprise" report at the end of 2024. Menlo Ventures was also an early investor in Anthropic, participating in its Series C financing round in 2023, and co-establishing the $100 million AI investment fund, Anthology Fund, with Anthropic in 2024. This list tallies globally unlisted AI companies with valuations exceeding $10 billion and publicly disclosed annualized revenues of over $100 million as of November 14. Thirty companies meet both criteria. The gap between the top "duopoly" continues to widen significantly. OpenAI remains in the lead with a valuation of approximately $1.25 trillion, while Anthropic closely follows at around $96.5 billion. The two have already created a trillion-dollar valuation chasm compared to their competitors. However, if ranked by annualized revenue, their positions have flipped: Anthropic has surpassed OpenAI. While they remain far ahead in valuation, the competition in revenue is seeing new shifts. Among Chinese companies, DeepSeek and Moonshot have entered the global top ten. DeepSeek ranks fifth with a $89 billion valuation, while Moonshot ranks seventh at $50 billion. According to the list's disclosed data, both companies have reached annualized revenues of approximately $1 billion. Nevertheless, looking at the overall list, the United States still holds an absolute advantage. Of the 30 companies, 23 are based in the US, covering multiple sectors including foundational models, AI programming, and cloud computing services. Two Chinese companies made the list, while the remaining five hail from Canada, France, Germany, and the UK respectively. At that time, there was still a revenue gap of more than double between the two companies. However, entering 2026, Anthropic's growth rate began to clearly surpass OpenAI's. As of the end of September this year, OpenAI's annualized revenue was approximately $50 billion; by the end of October, Anthropic's annualized revenue had reached $65 billion, overtaking OpenAI. AI Product.content: # Before you build another tool: How to choose the right level of AI for your CX stack. [Emily McReynolds](/blog/authors/emily-mcreynolds) ![](./media_18ef82c31cfbae2f6be545d425c69c70333e3b5a1.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium) The real measure of AI maturity in the enterprise isn’t how many advanced models you deploy or how many agents you build. It’s whether your teams can consistently select the right capability for their work and improve quality, efficiency, and returns. Like most enterprise technology decisions, making those choices well means putting the business need first and letting the capability follow. But the frenzy around AI has turned that logic on its head. I’ve seen conversations start with “we need AI” or “we need an agent” before anyone has defined what the AI is supposed to fix. This tendency gets reinforced by the way we talk about AI. It has become a catch-all term, treated as if it were a single capability that can be pointed at any process, rather than a range of different capabilities suited to different jobs. When those distinctions blur, it becomes easy to overshoot what the task needs, adding cost and complexity without improving the outcome. Most enterprises have already gone through a round of this, adopting the latest AI tools and increasing usage in the hope that results would follow. But Adobe’s *[State of AI Readiness](https://business.adobe.com/resources/sdk/state-of-ai-readiness.html)* report found that 58% of organizations remain stuck at the pilot or deployment stage with their AI projects. The answer isn’t to start over or use less AI. It’s to make better decisions about where, when, and how to use it. Takeaways drafted with AI from the article text. Alibaba has introduced Qwen4-Max, its latest flagship artificial intelligence (AI) model. Built on a new architecture with 2.4 trillion parameters and a 1-million-token context window, the model is designed for complex professional and scientific tasks. “It can take on a wide range of creative and professional work,” Alibaba said, citing applications in 3D modelling, game development, precision manufacturing, finance, law, healthcare, and scientific discovery. Qwen4-Max succeeds Qwen3.8-Max, which Alibaba launched in August. The company said the new model outperforms its predecessor across nearly every evaluated capability. In its Work360 evaluation, token usage fell by approximately 24% and 35% at Xhigh and High effort levels, respectively, the company claimed. Alibaba also reduced API prices, particularly for cached inputs. The average cost per task in its Work360 evaluation fell from $4.43 to $1.67—a 62% reduction. The earlier [Qwen3.8-Max launch](https://analyticsindiamag.com/ai-news/alibabas-qwen3-8-max-to-become-first-open-weight-max-model) marked another step in Alibaba's expansion of its AI model portfolio. The company also highlighted improvements in security testing. On Last Secure Code Bench, Qwen4-Max's function-level pass rate for both functionality and security increased from 22% for Qwen3.8-Max to 31.8%. The share of code meeting security requirements at the function, file, and repository levels rose from 8% to 14.7%. Alibaba said it had strengthened safeguards against cybersecurity misuse by retaining training data for defensive tasks, such as vulnerability detection and remediation, while removing data intended to improve offensive attack capabilities. Internal testing found no capabilities posing large-scale cybersecurity risks. For chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear risks, Alibaba introduced dedicated safety data during post-training. The company said internal evaluations found that the model identified more potentially harmful requests and provided safe responses, without significantly increasing users' ability to carry out harmful tasks. There are three models so far: **Inkling** (July 15, 2026), **Inkling-Small** (July 30) and **Inkling 2 Small**, announced on November 5 and released as open weights on November 12. The newest one scores **31** on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1. The original Inkling, a much bigger model, scores **12** on the same index. Most pages about Inkling were written in launch week in July, before the second generation existed and before Artificial Analysis rebuilt its index. That is why a score of 41 still circulates for the first model, and why some pages still quote the wrong parameter counts. This guide covers all three models with current numbers: what each one is, how good it is, what it costs, how to try it for free, and whether your Mac can run it. ## The Key Takeaways > * **Three models, one family:** Inkling (**975B** parameters, 41B active), Inkling-Small (**276B**, 12B active) and Inkling 2 Small (**594B**, 17B active), all under the **Apache 2.0** license. > * **The new one is the good one:** Inkling 2 Small scores **31** on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0.1, against **12** for Inkling and **13** for Inkling-Small. > * **Cheap to use, free to try:** Inkling 2 Small costs **$0.30 in and $1.00 out** per million tokens on Tinker and OpenRouter, and OpenRouter lists a **free variant**. > * **No consumer app:** the only first-party chat window is the developer-facing **Tinker Playground**. > * **Running it at home is hard:** the smallest Inkling 2 Small download is **171.7GB**, more memory than any MacBook has. ## What Is Inkling AI? Open Source AI.content: # Jailbroken PS4 runs 9-billion-parameter AI model at up to 43 tokens per second — open-source Garlic LLM bypasses drivers to talk directly to the 2013-era GPU It needs no PC and no internet, just a console running GoldHEN. Developer Leonardo Alegría’s open-source project Garlic LLM lets a jailbroken PS4 run the 9-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-9B AI model offline on the console’s 2013-era GPU. The app talks to the GPU directly, and the model is shrunk to about 4.5GiB to fit in the console’s memory, running at 31 to 39 tokens per second. The project, named after the memory the GPU reads directly — its sibling memory type is “Onion” — relies on a PS4 running GoldHEN, which is a homebrew enabler for exploited consoles. Garlic LLM is a free, single 5.66GB download, available on Hugging Face and installable through the PS4’s Package Installer, with about 6GB free needed, or 12GB if the package is first copied to the console’s internal disk. The developer tested it on a base/Slim PS4 on firmware 11.52. It’s capable of voice conversation, with spoken replies in seven languages through the Chatterbox speech model and the chat model running at about 22 tokens per second. A held controller button also lets it take dictation with Nvidia’s Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 speech-to-text model, which supports 25 European languages. Parakeet models also power local transcription and dictation apps such as Meetily and Hex. The main model is Alibaba’s small open-weight Qwen3.5-9B, which, at the claimed 31 to 39 tokens per second in text chat — the prompt and test method are not given — is usable on the console. The closest comparison is the PS5LM fork, which runs llama.cpp as a native app on the PS5 and reaches the console’s AMD GPU through PS5\_Vulkan, a port of the RADV driver. The open-source llama.cpp is a widely used program for running language models locally, and RADV is the open-source driver that lets AMD GPUs run Vulkan, the graphics and compute API. On the PS4 there is no such driver layer for homebrew; Garlic LLM uses neither llama.cpp nor a Vulkan port, or so it would appear. The model’s operations, such as matrix multiplies over 4-bit weights, are compute kernels written in OpenCL C and compiled with LLVM for AMD’s Graphics Core Next (GCN) architecture. The weights are kept in that “Garlic” memory, while the CPU side, in plain C, handles the tokenizer, the interface, text rendering, and audio. The pipeline runs from the prompt to the CPU tokenizer, then, for each token, a PM4 command buffer — the low-level commands a graphics driver would normally generate, which, in this case, the app builds itself — and the GCN kernels, before the token is displayed or spoken. The whole thing is built with the open-source OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain. One immediate question is how you fit a 9-billion-parameter model in the console’s 8GB of memory, which the CPU and GPU share. At 8 bits per weight, you have one byte per parameter, meaning you’d need at least 9GB, with typically more than that required overall. Part of the answer is 4-bit (“Q4”) weights, which take half as much, although 3-bit (“Q3”) weights, at about 3.5 bits with scales, are used for the two largest matrices in each layer. Using the combination gets you to about 4.5GiB, versus about 4.9GiB if it were all 4-bit. The attention, or KV, cache is also 4-bit, which lets a 16K-token context fit, in comparison to the model’s native 256K. The Parakeet dictation model adds 0.33GiB and the Chatterbox voice models 0.29GiB and 0.09GiB, for a grand total of 5.23GiB, or 5.62GB, which closely matches the 5.66GB package size. Qwen3.5 comes with a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, and Garlic LLM uses it to draft up to two tokens ahead, with the full model verifying. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![withcoral Releases Coral, an Open-Source Gateway for Controlled Agent Tool Use](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fwithcoral-releases-coral-an-open-source-gateway-for-controlled-agent-tool-use_gen_1794844187981-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #AI # withcoral Releases Coral, an Open-Source Gateway for Controlled Agent Tool Use • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •5 min read Share this article Advertisement [Advertise on LavX NewsSee options](/advertise) Coral sits between AI agents and the systems they touch, letting agents write short TypeScript programs to call tools, save the ones that work as reusable custom tools, and run every call through an Allow, Ask, or Block policy. withcoral ships it under the Apache 2.0 license with desktop and self-hosted server options. Coral, an open-source gateway from withcoral, lets AI agents write short TypeScript programs to call tools and save the ones that work. The project, hosted at [github.com/withcoral/coral](https://github.com/withcoral/coral), targets a gap withcoral identifies in most MCP gateways: they decide only which tools an agent can see, then hand over the keys. withcoral started Coral while building an AI SRE. Investigations spanned telemetry across internal and external systems, needed broad permissions and many tokens, and started from scratch each time. Coral stores the route once a task succeeds, so the agent reuses it. ## The problem with all-or-nothing tool access Most MCP gateways filter which tools an agent sees. That leaves two states: full access or none. If an agent can call update\_record, it can update any record in any way the tool allows. Coral adds a third option: a custom tool is code, so it can encode rules the Allow and Block settings cannot. closeStaleTicket can change one field, and only on tickets with no activity for 30 days. You set Allow, Ask, or Block on the custom tool like any other tool, and Coral still checks every provider call inside it against policy. ## How Coral runs code To use tools, an agent writes a short TypeScript program. One program can call several tools, filter results, and return only what the task needs, so less raw data passes through the model's context. Coral runs each program in a fresh V8 isolate with no network access, no credentials, and no imports. It checks every tool call against the workspace policy, adds credentials, and forwards the call to the provider. A policy can require a person to approve the call. Every run carries the name of the person or agent that started it. The agent sends programs through the exec tool. It calls coral.search to find usable tools and read their TypeScript signatures, then sends a program that does the work. This example finds open pull requests with no reviewer and posts them to Slack: ``` const { data: pulls } = await coral.providers.github.pulls.list({ owner: "withcoral", repo: "coral", state: "open", }); const unreviewed = pulls.filter((pull) => pull.requested_reviewers.length === 0); await coral.providers.slack.chat.postMessage({ channel: "#engineering", text: unreviewed.map((pull) => `#${pull.number} ${pull.title}`).join("\n"), }); return unreviewed.map((pull) => pull.number); ``` If posting to Slack needs approval, the run pauses there until a human approves it. The agent receives the pull request numbers, not the full GitHub response. The run happens on the Coral server, so it continues even if the agent disconnects. ## Custom tools that stick The agent saves a successful program as a private tool and calls it next time in one step as coral.private.({ ... }). Agents find custom tools in the same search as provider tools, and reuse or edit them instead of starting over. Developers are free to study and alter every line, test it on personal hardware, or deploy a private copy to Cloudflare Workers through their accounts. Published on November 13 in a [company blog post](https://blog.cloudflare.com/kitesurf-open-source/), the release fulfills an open-source commitment [Cloudflare](https://betanews.com/topic/cloudflare/) first voiced at Kitesurf’s [August debut](https://blog.cloudflare.com/kitesurf/). “That promise is now real,” the company wrote. > Kitesurf is now open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. Fork the repo, run it locally with Wrangler, or deploy a custom instance to Cloudflare. https://t.co/y7V8xJoUO4 > > — Cloudflare Changelog (@CFchangelog) [November 13, 2026](https://x.com/CFchangelog/status/2121362696587149656?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) [Apache 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) permits anyone to modify the code and use it commercially. A [September update](https://blog.cloudflare.com/kitesurf-update/) had already brought WebMCP support, fresh APIs and wider site compatibility to the engine. Everything runs inside Workers, the company’s [serverless platform](https://betanews.com/article/cloudflare-has-acquired-deno-and-will-use-it-to-boost-workers/), with no browser container involved. Pages get their HTML parsed, styles applied and scripts executed before Kitesurf produces a screenshot. Because the engine implements the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), which automation software relies on to control Chrome, Puppeteer can hook into it directly. MCP clients and Playwright can also connect over WebSocket, Cloudflare said. Lower CPU and memory demands than a full Chromium build are the goal, with the browser still expected to load sites, run scripts and work with page elements. Elastic scaling throughout the Workers network is another aim. Assembled from open-source Rust projects compiled into WebAssembly (a portable code format that Workers can execute), the engine draws on five main components. Blitz covers the DOM, HTML parsing, page layout and painting, and Stylo processes stylesheets from parsing through the cascade to computed values. Boa, a JavaScript engine running inside WebAssembly, steps in only as a fallback when code cannot execute in Dynamic Workers. Krilla handles PDF export, and Linebender libraries draw 2D graphics and lay out text. Every included project keeps its original license, and a NOTICE file in the codebase spells out those outside terms. Internally, the design has a three-part structure. SkillEvaluator gives teams a staged way to check the instructions and files they give AI agents. It combines checks on a skill with comparisons of agent runs with and without that skill, so teams can assess its quality and effect on task results. ![The README of the NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator repository on GitHub](https://news.lavx.hu/api/media/file/nvidia-skillevaluator-readme-2026-11-16.jpg) *Screenshot: the project's README on GitHub* ## What it is SkillEvaluator is a Python framework for checking AI agent skills, the folders of instructions and supporting files that guide an agent through work. It helps authors assess whether those materials meet quality and safety expectations, whether their guidance overlaps with other skills, and whether a skill changes task results. The project treats evaluation as a staged process: a team can start with checks on the skill itself, then compare agent behavior when it needs evidence about the skill’s effect. The framework addresses two related questions: whether a skill has sound, compatible instructions, and whether an agent performs better on a task with that skill available. Skill authors can examine one skill on its own or compare it with a catalog. Teams can also run an agent against task cases and compare its results with and without the skill. These evaluations give teams distinct evidence about the skill’s contents and its influence on agent work. ## How it works SkillEvaluator separates its work into three tiers. Tier 1 checks a skill’s structure, safety and compatibility with agent harnesses. Tier 2 looks for repeated or overlapping guidance, including comparisons across a skill catalog. Tier 3 evaluates an agent while it works on tasks. Each tier can run on its own, and teams can combine them when they want a broader assessment. Tier 1 combines static checks with optional model-based checks. The project can use external scanners for security coverage; if a scanner cannot run, the result is marked incomplete. Teams can also use a model provider for language-model checks. Tier 2 uses embeddings and chat to examine overlap, while a catalog enables comparisons between skills. The two tiers focus on the skill materials rather than an agent’s live task performance. Tier 3 runs an agent in a sandbox and measures its task results. The team supplies a supported agent, provider access and a running sandbox, then evaluates cases grounded in the skill or other task sources. Open Source AI.content: Threat Intelligence # GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold November 16, 2026 ##### Google Threat Intelligence Group ##### Google Threat Intelligence Visibility and context on the threats that matter most. [Contact Us & Get a Demo](https://cloud.google.com/security/resources/google-threat-intelligence-demo?utm_source=cgc-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=FY25-Q2-global-GCP30649-website-su-dgcsm-GTI-interest) Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor --- ### Executive Summary As threat actors [increasingly move beyond basic prompting](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai?e=48754805) to deploying autonomous multi-agent [frameworks](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/artex-and-friends-enter-agentic-offensive-frameworks), automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like [LLMJacking](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/llmjacking-monetizing-compromised-cloud-models/?e=48754805), the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. Key trends over the last quarter include: * **Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks:** Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as [ARTEX](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/artex-and-friends-enter-agentic-offensive-frameworks), CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. * **Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation:** Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention. * **Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse**: Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from [LLMJacking](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/llmjacking-monetizing-compromised-cloud-models) by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers). * **LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO):** State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution. * **Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution:** Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution. Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild. [Jensen Huang](/tag/jensen+huang), co-founder of [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia), resigned as the company's president, chief executive, and board member on November 12, ending 33 years at its helm. Chief Financial Officer [Colette Kress](/tag/colette+kress) has assumed the role of interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor. This leadership change followed a probe into Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, reportedly suspected of passing information to Beijing. ### AI infrastructure risks The leadership transition introduces four risks for AI data centre plans. These include key-person risk in the GPU roadmap and closer scrutiny of GPU shipments to Southeast Asia. There is also a loss of political capital in Washington and a potential pullback in Nvidia's financing of the AI industry. Nvidia shares plunged more than 12 per cent on the day of the resignation before recovering, extending declines as the leadership turmoil weighed on the sector. Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company reportedly bought at least $4.8 billion of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026. US officials had previously investigated whether the company helped China obtain restricted chips. The resignation compounds pressure on data centres following recent midterm elections where voters opposed data centre development in many local contests. Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on November 17, its first since Huang's exit. House committees have summoned Huang for a closed-door interview regarding Megaspeed, chip diversion, and Nvidia's security protocols. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

Infra & Chips.content: [Home](/en) Article # Expectations for AI chips have been sharply lowered. 半导体行业观察2026-11-17 09:41 A clear shift is taking place in the growth expectations for AI infrastructure investment. There is a noticeable shift underway in the growth expectations for AI infrastructure investment. On November 13, semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis released its latest model adjustment, sharply downgrading forecasts for global AI accelerator capital expenditure, chip shipments, HBM demand and power consumption in the coming years. Among them, the 2028 global AI accelerator capital expenditure expectation was cut from the previous $1.054 trillion to $758 billion, a 28% reduction; the 2030 figure was reduced from $1.531 trillion to $923 billion, a roughly 40% drop. In this round of adjustments, NVIDIA has become the company most affected. ([NYSE:VRT](/equities/gs-acquisition-a)) opened the ATLAS Lab, a facility designed to test power and cooling systems for AI data centers before computing hardware becomes commercially available, according to a company statement. The Advanced Test Lab for Architecture and Systems uses workload emulation and digital modeling to test infrastructure against simulated [NVIDIA](/equities/nvidia-corp) accelerated computing architectures. The lab incorporates digital twin workflows within the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, including NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA DSX Sim. The facility operates as a representative pod of an AI data center, testing power, thermal management, controls and IT infrastructure together. Vertiv stated the validated designs can be applied at larger scale deployments. "ATLAS lets us find and solve integration issues before they reach a customer site," said Scott Armul, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Vertiv. The lab addresses what the company identifies as five technical challenges in AI infrastructure: density, speed, scale, complexity and dynamic load profiles. Testing occurs at the system level rather than validating individual products separately. Vertiv and NVIDIA held a ribbon-cutting event on Nov. 6, where engineering teams from both companies evaluated power, liquid cooling and controls systems responding to emulated AI workload behavior. "By bringing NVIDIA AI factory architecture requirements together with Vertiv’s power and cooling expertise, our teams can identify and resolve infrastructure challenges earlier," said Vladimir Troy, Vice President of AI Infrastructure at NVIDIA. The lab tests infrastructure from grid interconnection to rack level, including liquid cooling at the chip and heat rejection systems. Vertiv stated this approach allows customers to resolve technical issues before deploying physical equipment. However, analysts say financial institutions are demanding long-term customer contracts and additional guarantees rather than GPU collateral in new deals, which could make it harder for financially weaker neocloud companies to secure funding. Morgan Stanley raised the possibility that capital will concentrate among large hyperscalers, while JPMorgan expects delays in closing new deals and expanded demands for compensation. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia's $500 Billion AI Financing Vision Survives, but Wall Street Demands More Guarantees for Neoclouds](https://img.biggo.com/aWG-POpf1pb_0N_jn_pnZKXvTTrTEzGs3gu25jGdKWk/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExL2ZiYjNmMjliLTQ3MzMtNDVmYS1iNTRiLWFkMGNlZDQ4MTc0NV8xNzk0ODgwODAyX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia's $500 billion external financing initiative for AI infrastructure is expected to survive the CEO transition, but the flow and terms of the money are likely to change. As Wall Street financial institutions demand long-term customer contracts and additional guarantees in new deals, neocloud companies with relatively thin financial foundations are finding it harder to secure funding. According to foreign media reports on the 16th (local time), global financial institutions working with Nvidia are continuing discussions on AI infrastructure investment, and no signal of a business halt has come from Nvidia. However, the outlet did not rule out the possibility that the initiative could be temporarily suspended during Nvidia's early review of its operating direction. In August, Nvidia announced a partnership with six financial institutions — Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR — to build an AI infrastructure financing platform. The structure supplies external capital to AI data center projects that use Nvidia GPUs, with financial institutions assessing the risk of individual projects and providing funding. The long-term goal is to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital. The program has served as a growth ladder for neocloud companies that rent out AI computing resources. Companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius require massive upfront capital for GPU purchases and data center construction, making them highly dependent on external financing. Nvidia has supported some neoclouds by investing directly, guaranteeing minimum revenue for certain computing capacity, and sharing a portion of excess profits. Neoclouds secured revenue stability, while Nvidia captured both GPU sales and computing service revenue. The problem is that the risk allocation in this structure is shifting. Financial institutions are signaling that they will weigh customers' long-term usage contracts and financial guarantees more heavily than the collateral value of the GPUs themselves. They are demanding contract structures that allow them to recover principal even if data center construction is delayed or demand falters. For neoclouds with limited cash generation of their own, failure to secure additional guarantees or long-term customer contracts could slow the pace of GPU adoption and data center expansion.
